title: I LAUGH YOU: When Laughter Cuts Sharper Than the Brush
excerpt: When art is sold like a late-night infomercial, laughter is the only weapon left. An analysis of the subversive power of humor inside the capitalism of the galleries.
content:
Christian Jankowski showed us the playbook back in 2008, and we learned absolutely nothing. When the VernissageTV hosts at Art Cologne began hawking artworks like mattresses on a late-night shopping channel — “This wonderful object, only three left!” — it was meant as parody. Today, nearly two decades later, it has hardened into business as usual. The art market never got the joke. Or worse: it absorbed it, packaged it, and resold it for $777 apiece.

We live in an era in which the market no longer passes judgment on the artwork; the artwork merely exists because the market permits it. And that is exactly why we have to start laughing. Not out of joy. Out of subversive self-defense.

The Shopping Channel of Longing

Jankowski’s Kunstmarkt TV (2018), grounded in that legendary live performance at Art Cologne 2008, exposed the great self-deception of the scene. The principle was simple and lethal: take the aesthetic aura of a work, compress it into thirty seconds of pitching time, throw in a phone number for impulse buyers — and the disenchantment is complete. The interactive format allowed real-time online bidding; viewers could close the deal with a single click while prices ticked upward on live camera. It was a perfect mirror of what we now politely call the “contemporary art world”: a home-shopping channel for longings nobody actually wants fulfilled.

The brutality of the joke lies in its truth. Walk the fair halls today and you no longer see art. You see inventory. Positions. Liquidity reserves in frames. And when reality has become so absurd that satire can no longer be told apart from it, laughter is the only adequate response. It is the flight forward.

From Corinth to the Cash Register

Laughter in art has a lineage. Lovis Corinth’s Laughing Girl of 1883, or the impish figures of Franz von Stuck — laughter once served as contrast, as a yes to life against death, as joy against heaviness. It was a laughter that still had nothing to hide. In Corinth, laughter still broke stereotypes; it was rebellious because it was female and untamed.

Today we laugh differently. We laugh because otherwise we would have to scream. The 24,236 fragments into which an artist’s self-portrait can be shattered are not just physical shards. They are 24,236 small bursts of laughter, pushing back against the nonsense. Each one available from $77 to $777 — a price spectrum that could not be more absurd. Who is actually buying whom here? Are we buying the artist, or buying ourselves back as conformists?

The irony is impeccable: the more that is bought, the less remains, and the more expensive becomes the thing nobody wanted. In the end it is the ugliest, most abstract fragments that fetch the highest prices — not because they are beautiful, but because they are scarce. Value emerges not from meaning but from manufactured scarcity. That is no longer art. That is a joke with dead eyes.

I LAUGH YOU — The Bared Teeth of the System

This is where the project we are watching steps in. It takes the mechanism seriously enough to push it into absurdity. If capitalism turns every meaning into merchandise, then the most radical answer is not the solemn face of protest but the wide grin of someone who has seen through the game. I LAUGH YOU — this is no declaration of love in the conventional sense. It is the recognition that, sometimes, the only way to save what you love is to laugh it off the stage.

The abstraction of the individual image fragments plays a double role here. They are literally pieces of the artist — his skin, his eyes, his paint — and at the same time entirely empty of meaning without the viewer. Every buyer projects their own meaning into them, their own narrative. This is the ultimate democratization and, at the same time, the ultimate con: we buy a piece of a human being we do not understand and call it an investment.

Daniel Hug, the man behind Art Cologne, distrusts the “global art market machine.” He bets on local galleries, on progressive art, on the attempt to think outside the big money. The student art market — those expressive, abstract gateway drugs for collectors — is meant to open alternative markets beyond capitalism. And yet absorption lurks here too. Laughter, then, has to be more persistent than the system.

He Who Laughs Last Holds the Highest Hammer

The subversive power of humor in this context lies not in the joke itself but in its persistence. While the market tries to swallow everything, laughter remains ungraspable. It is the moment when the buyer realizes that for $777 he has literally acquired a piece of a face that is laughing at him. A piece that says: You bought me, but you will never own me.

In a world where art explicitly trades on the value of things — even though value only exists because art exists — every fragment sold is a small act of sabotage. The artist laughs through his own splintered features. He laughs the market off the stage by offering himself as commodity — completely, radically, unmistakably. And we, the viewers, the buyers, the collectors, are forced to laugh along. Not because it is funny. But because the alternative would be silence. And silence was bought up by the market a long time ago.

In the end, only the fragment remains. The small, square piece of paint that looks at us and laughs. And we no longer ask: what is this worth? But: who, exactly, is laughing at whom here?
